entries.title: About the Course
entries.content:
This course includes the following topic(s): U.S. History: Grades 7-8, Ancient History: Grades 7-9

About U.S. History: Grades 7-8
Read about U.S. history from 1800-1900 through books that immerse students in the time period and allow them to see the world through the eyes of those who lived it. Through engaging narratives, history spines, primary source documents, and books that show different perspectives, students come to see history as more than dates and events and develop relationships with people from the past. Viewing images, looking at maps, and working on one's Book of Centuries are also part of developing this relationship.

About World History: Grades 7-9
Read about U.S. and world history from 800-1650AD and ancient history from 3500-550BC through biographies, primary source documents, and history spines. View images and reference atlases and maps to set the people and events in their time and place. Update History Charts and Book of Centuries as appropriate for student level., Read about Canadian and world history from 800-1650AD and ancient history from 3500-550BC through biographies, primary source documents, and history spines. View images and reference atlases and maps to set the people and events in their time and place. Update History Charts and Book of Centuries as appropriate for student level., Read about U.S. and world history from 800-1650AD and ancient history from 3500-550BC through biographies, primary source documents, and history spines. View images and reference atlases and maps to set the people and events in their time and place. Update History Charts and Book of Centuries.

About Ancient History: Grades 7-9
Read about ancient history from 100 BC-350 AD through biographies, primary source documents, and history spines. Students will view images, reference maps, and update their Book of Centuries as part of the lessons.

blocks.text:
• Read through the lesson and gather any necessary links. 

• If you have not read the book, you may want to read the selected pages in advance. 

• Decide which lessons/books to read together and which to have students read independently.

• Connect back to the previous lesson. Have students give a summary of what they remember. (Full narration is not necessary.)

• If the previous passage is difficult to remember, teachers may ask a leading question: "What can you tell me about..." Or students may try looking back at any chapter/section headings or illustrations or reading the first paragraph to jog the memory.

• Use a picture, map, or engaging question to pique the student's interest in the day's lesson (often included in lesson plans). 

• If necessary, talk about a few unfamiliar words that will be crucial to understanding.

• Read the day's passage out loud or have the student read independently. Sometimes reading for the specified time is a better guide.

• If a book is challenging, try stopping to narrate every now and then rather than waiting until the end. It can also help to read aloud. Or you might want to use an audiobook version of the text and have students read along with it.

• Have students keep an eye out for events or characters to add to their Citizenship Notebook, Book of Centuries, or Copywork Book.

• Have students retell the passage orally or write a narration. 

• Alternatively, students might analyze a character, trace cause to consequence, outline a passage, or use one of the other methods indicated by Charlotte Mason in School Education Chapter 16, especially p.180.

• Students who enjoy writing can experiment with different types of written narrations, but this is not required.

• Give the student an opportunity to share thoughts on the lesson and any connections made (orally or in writing). 

• You could ask them what they thought about the passage or ask an open-ended question to stimulate discussion. Discussion questions are often included in the lesson plans.
• Optional: Add something to the Book of Centuries, Century Chart, Citizenship Notebook, or Commonplace book. If students would like to include pictures, these may be drawn or printed.

⍞ Materials: PDF Link

➜ INTRO

lessons.title: 30m Ancient History: Grades 7-9 - Lesson 1
lessons.body:
Meeting Sulla
⍞ Materials: A Short History of Ancient Rome, Historical Atlas of the World

➜ INTRO
This year, you are learning about ancient Rome. We are not starting at the beginning with the legend of Romulus and Remus in 753 B.C. We are jumping ahead to 88 BC. The Roman Republic has become a world power. It has marched through the Greek world, razed cities like Carthage, and unseated powerful people. As Pascal Hughes says, "The march of Rome appears unstoppable." 
However, what had once been a republic, which had enabled certain people to vote in their leadership, was quickly becoming more of a dictatorship, which is where one person assumes absolute power. There were a number of factors that led to Sulla becoming the first dictator in the Roman Republic. He assumed power through political violence, manipulation of land and resources, and military coups. In 88 BC, the Republic found itself in danger. 
Sulla's story doesn't start at the beginning of his dictatorship. 

➜ READ, NARRATE & DISCUSS
Ch.6 p.89-99 - end at "political violence tamed" 

➜ LOCATE
⍞ Map Resource: Historical Atlas of the World, p.14-15. 
Find Carthage, Rome, and any other cities that pop up in your reading to familiarize yourself with the world of Ancient Rome.

lessons.body:
The Beginning of the Story
⍞ Materials: Sacajawea

➜ INTRO
By the age of 16, Sacajawea had been kidnapped from her tribe, gambled away to be a man's second wife, and was pregnant with that man's baby. That's when she would join the journey of Meriwether Lewis and William Clark down the Mississippi River and to the Pacific Ocean. But, where did her story begin? 

Joseph Bruchac will explore the early life of Sacajawea as well as recount her journey with Lewis and Clark, which became one of the most famous expeditions to take place in American History. While it is well researched and Joseph Bruchac uses primary sources like the journals of Lewis and Clark as support for the story, it remains a work of fiction. There is much that we don't know about Sacajawea's story.

➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS
Begin with the "Author's Note" p.195-199. 
Read the Prologue and Ch.1.

• How different would Sacajawea's life have been if she had stayed amongst her people?

lessons.title: 30m Ancient History: Grades 7-9 - Lesson 3
lessons.body:
Spartacus and a Revolt
⍞ Materials: A Short History of Ancient Rome, Historical Atlas of the World

➜ INTRO
Rome was built on slavery. In 73 BC, there were more than a million people enslaved in Rome's Italian lands. As Pascal Hughes says, "Some have been bought from foreign merchants, others taken by military conquest, or enslaved as a punishment for criminality. Then there are the unfortunates who were born into bondage, or who are the victims of kidnap by slavers, or who could see no other option in life than to sell themselves into servitude."
However, revolution came to Rome, and it was led by a slave named Spartacus. There are modern-day movies that praise the bravery of this man and those who rose up with him against the powers that shackled them. Spartacus' story is fraught with bravery and peril, yet it left him a legend in the history books. 

➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS
Ch.7 p.110-118 - stop at "Third Servile War" 

• How did Spartacus' actions influence the Roman Empire?

Trail of Tears
⍞ Materials: PDF link

➜ INTRO
The settlers wanted more land. The Native American Tribes inhabited this land. So between 1816 and 1840, Tribes, including Cherokees, Chickasaws, Creeks, Seminoles, and Choctaws, signed treaties that gave up their land to the US. Around 1829, Andrew Jackson and Congress passed an act called the Indian Removal Act that forced remaining tribes to move west. There were over 100,000 Native Americans who were forced from their homes to make a journey that many of them would not survive.

⍞ Materials: A Short History of Ancient Rome, Historical Atlas of the World

The story of Julius Caesar captured audiences' attention then, and it remains prominent in our modern-day culture. The blood, betrayal, and scandal of the story is what has led to this story's permanence. But as you will read, there is more to this story. Julius Caesar becomes a famous leader for a number of reasons. As you read through the story retold by Pascal Hughes, consider the many reasons Julius Caesar's story might attract so much attention.

⍞ Materials: Sacajawea

➜ NOTE
We are skipping Ch.13-15 for the sake of time.

➜ INTRO
Sacajawea found herself able to help the expedition in more ways than just translating for her people. Growing up in the village, she knew that there would come a time when it would be impossible to hunt and that the survival of people depended on finding food in other ways. Mainly, she taught them how to forage for edible roots.

There would be more difficulties than just running low on food. One of the largest would be grizzly bears. Even though Lewis and Clark were outfitted with guns and bullets, they had a hard time taking down the grizzlies, which caused Captain Lewis to say, “these bears being so hard to die rather intimidates me.” A canoe nearly sank, animals charged their tents, and Sacajawea came down with an illness.

⍞ Materials: Gold Mountain

➜ INTRO
This historical novel is based on the building of the transcontinental railroad, which took place from 1863-1869. It was an arduous, dangerous job for the men who signed up to do it. Historians estimate that at any one time as many as 10,000 to 15,000 Chinese were working on constructing the railroad. It took more than four years to complete the western section of the railroad and connect the coasts. This story will bring this time period to life and give you a glimpse of what those workers endured so they could send money back to their families in China. Upon completion of the railroad, some workers went back to China; others stayed in America to work in agriculture, mining, logging, or domestic service or work in manufacturing to produce cigars and other items.

➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS
1. Read author's note p.274-276
2. p.1-12 beginning - "to say or do."

• What customs or traditions in Chinese culture have you noticed so far?”

➜ BACKGROUND
1. Foot binding — the practice of applying tight binding to the feet of young girls to prevent further growth — was a Chinese custom historically associated with the wealthy. Small feet were considered more attractive and, therefore, necessary to find a more suitable partner. It was banned in 1911, but the practice continued in rural areas until circa 1949, when women were forced to remove the bindings on their “lotus feet” by governmental decree.

Today, we will look at another architectural style influenced by the Old World—Gothic Revival. These homes in the 1800s were romantic adaptations of medieval architecture. Delicate wooden ornaments and other decorative details suggested the architecture of medieval England. - Grouped chimneys
- Pinnacles (spires or peaks)
- Leaded glass

The Christian Revolution
⍞ Materials: The Witness of Early Christian Women: Mothers of the Church

➜ INTRO
How revolutionary was Christianity in the Roman Empire? Jesus' teachings challenged a lot of different ideas that had come to be accepted as truths, such as the belief that women were inferior. Mike Aquilina writes, "Males were superior (a man would say) because women were inferior. It was obvious — so obvious that it hardly needed an argument. Fire is hot, water is wet, and women are inferior to men. This unquestioned and unquestionable truth was the basis of all human society."
So what happens when one of Christianity's most prolific writers challenges this idea in his letters? Think about Galatians 3:28, which reads, "There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus." Paul's words would have registered as an attack on Rome's family values.  
Paul promotes the idea that women have a place in society, a place in the Bible, and a place in the early church. As you read through this book, we encourage you to take note of anything that stands out, anything you agree with, and anything you disagree with.

lessons.title: 30m U.S. History: Grades 7-8 - Lesson 57
lessons.body:
Louis Hughes in the Spring
⍞ Materials: A Year in the South: 1865

➜ INTRO
Like many enslaved women and men, Louis Hughes had dreams of being free. He would run away a couple of times, and every time he received a punishment. His story highlights the evil that we must face as those who study history. Humans are capable of great evil towards each other. Sin is a part of the human experience, and we can trace it to every place and every time.

In his book, Why Study History, John Fea writes, "Indeed, anyone who studies the past realizes that there are no heroes in history. While people may perform heroic acts, all humans are tainted by sin and are susceptible to acting in ways that preference themselves over others and God. Historians understand, perhaps better than most, the reality of the pain, suffering, injustice, anger, and vice brought on by sin. In other words, they understand the tragic dimensions of life."

History reminds us of the inherent weakness in the human condition and the very real possibility that our fellow human beings are capable of horrendous things. This should humble us, for “there, but for the grace of God, go I.” One day, there will be a new heaven and new earth where there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain.

➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS
p.109-118 stop at “and poultry alike."

• How does Louis Hughes' story tell you more about what's going on in his community?

Perpetua lived in the time of Emperor Septimius Severus. Mike Aquilina wrote that Septimius Severus "wasn't persecuting Christians per se at the moment, but he had made it a capital crime for Roman citizens to become Jews or Christians." Perpetua was a noblewoman and was able to write and read. She converted to Christianity and was sentenced to die with her servant Felicity. Her story is different from other accounts because it was written by her own hand. As you read through it, what kind of questions do you have for Perpetua and Felicity?

lessons.body:
Cornelia McDonald and Louis Hughes in Fall
⍞ Materials: A Year in the South: 1865

➜ INTRO
1865 was a year marked by many uncertainties. As men and women were freed from the bondage of slavery, they would need to find homes, jobs, and safe havens where they could relish their freedom. And households that had built their wealth on the backs of slaves would need to transition quickly to be able to sustain themselves. The year 1865 would be one of the most tumultuous years in the history of the United States, but the fight for freedom didn't end with the Emancipation Proclamation or the winning of the Civil War. The rest of the 1800s would be filled with a struggle for equality that was just beginning.

➜ READ, NARRATE, & DISCUSS
p.204-217 start at “She sat down” - end of chapter

• Compare Cornelia McDonald's fall to Louis Hughes' fall.
